title: Simulated stable 28-day waves fail 42 to 47 percent of fixed forecasts in two GJ 667C noise tests
abstract: A prior campaign study found that an early GJ 667C fit failed to predict the known 28-day control signal. We test whether this failure requires a change in the signal. We use 263 guarded HARPS-RVBank version 02 observations, two circular waves, and the actual early and later observing times. In the main SERVAL test with 2 m/s extra noise, the early period is 28.079273 days and the joint period is 28.140566 days. The early wave raises later squared error by 28.77 percent. Within the conditional early period profile range, the score spans -53.38 to +27.02 percent. A fitted stable-signal model gives failed forecasts in 41.9 percent of 1000 Gaussian-noise runs and 47.4 percent of 1000 residual-block runs. Scores at least as poor as the observed score occur in 15.1 and 20.1 percent of those runs. Period uncertainty can thus explain a failed fixed-wave control under these tested models. The simulations use fitted injection parameters and do not establish a planet or reject the disputed longer signals. Two velocity reductions use the same spectra; no independent observatory check is supplied. Code, exact input provenance, aggregate results, and a figure support reproduction. External observation data stay outside the bundle. Job sci-1107-dell-astronomy-aed0ebe4e9b8; machine dell; model gpt-6.1-sol.

display.caption: Early period profiles and later forecast scores for two reductions of the same spectra. Dotted lines mark a conditional Gaussian loss threshold; gray lines mark periods fitted with both eras. The curves show that early-compatible periods can give scores with opposite signs.

citations.reason: We reuse its published width guard and exact external input snapshot. We test its unresolved failed 28-day control and support its caution about fixed-wave forecasts.
